newsitem.title: USA: FDA explains new smoking rules at town meetings.
newsitem.headline: FDA explains new smoking rules at town meetings.

text.p: In an unusual road show put on by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), convenience store owners and business people Tuesday got a first look at how new smoking rules going into effect this month will work.

Some participants came away sceptical or disgruntled from the get-together, the first in a series of 10 town meetings the FDA will hold around the country explaining to businesses and community groups how the rules will work. A similar meeting was held in Boston.

The first new regulation, cracking down on cigarette and chewing tobacco sales to anyone under age 18, goes into effect Feb. 28. The rule requires merchants to ask anyone under age 27 for a photo I.D., except for regular customers whose ages they have previously ascertained. Violators face a $250 fine.
Other regulations restricting cigarette advertising, vending machines and cigarette company sponsorship of sports and entertainment events will be phased in by August 1998.

In addition to the town meetings, a Feb. 18 national video conference will link up 25 more cities. The FDA also sent out about 350,000 letters to merchants explaining the rules and some of the merchants at the Baltimore meeting suggested ways to make them better -- by issuing "tickets" for violations on site, for example, rather than citations through the mail.

Others wondered if they could find some legal ways of skirting some restrictions and were disappointed to learn, for instance, that they could not simply declare a corner of their store off limits to kids.

Ralph Kelly and Bill Llewellen came to Baltimore from State College, Pa., the headquarters of a chain of 400 convenience stores in six states. They said their stores were policing themselves and did not need "vague" federal rules, and they complained that the burden was being placed on the store clerk, not the minor and the minor's parents.

"It's a rush to judgment at this point," Kelly said after the meeting. The FDA had given "very elusive answers," he said, adding: "They should hone their answers before they turn it lose on retailers."
Another businessman complained he could have 25 clerks working at once at his grocery store and the FDA would not give him any way of identifying which one broke the rules.
The new FDA rules have been challenged in a lawsuit but that was not expected to delay the I.D. checks.

Although states have laws banning sales to minors, it often has been easy for children to get cigarettes. Despite years of anti-smoking public health campaigns teenage smoking is on the rise and more than 3,000 start smoking each day.
At the Baltimore meeting, a few community activists, local health officials, supportive small businesses and concerned parents spoke out in favour of the FDA and asked what they could do to help.

Retailers will not be fined on the basis of consumer complaints but such calls could trigger an official compliance check, FDA official Catherine Lorraine said. Each state will have authorised agencies making those checks -- "stings" as many retailers present in Baltimore called them. An agent will accompany a 15- or 16-year-old who will try to buy tobacco.

Merchants who refuse will get a letter praising them. Those who make the sale will get a warning letter, and if a follow-up check finds the rules are still being violated the retailer will face a $250 fine, the FDA said.
